concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of Parliamentary Privileges: Articles 105 and 194
key_dimensions: Article 105 for Parliament vs. Article 194 for State Legislatures — parallel but distinct provisions
Pre-44th Amendment position: privileges co-extensive with House of Commons vs. Post-44th Amendment: privileges as defined by Parliament itself
The gap problem: Parliament has not codified privileges by law, so pre-amendment House of Commons position still applies by default
UPSC trap: Article 105(3) says 'as may from time to time be defined by Parliament' — but no such law exists yet

concepts.name: Freedom of Speech within Parliament: Scope and Absolute Nature
key_dimensions: Article 105(1): Complete immunity from court proceedings for anything said or vote cast inside Parliament
Distinction from Article 19(1)(a): Parliamentary speech is absolute, not subject to reasonable restrictions
Covers speeches, votes, committee proceedings, but NOT speeches made outside Parliament (even if reporting a parliamentary event)
UPSC trap: A member can be tried for bribery related to speech (PV Narasimha Rao case — majority held immunity; later revisited in 2024 Sita Soren case)

concepts.name: Immunity from Court Proceedings: Article 105(2) and its Limits
key_dimensions: No court can question the validity of proceedings in Parliament — courts cannot scrutinize legislative debates
Distinction between 'proceedings in Parliament' (protected) vs. acts outside Parliament (not protected)
Does not protect a member against criminal prosecution for acts committed outside the House
UPSC trap: Immunity extends to publication of reports/papers under authority of the House, not unauthorized publications

concepts.name: Bribery and Parliamentary Privilege: The PV Narasimha Rao to Sita Soren Evolution
key_dimensions: PV Narasimha Rao case (1998): 5-judge bench held members who voted (even for bribe) had immunity; those who took bribe but did not vote had no immunity — created perverse incentive
Sita Soren case (2024): 7-judge Constitutional Bench unanimously overruled PV Narasimha Rao — bribery for vote/speech NOT protected by privilege
Rationale: Privilege exists to protect Parliament's functioning, not to shield corruption
UPSC high-yield: This is a landmark reversal — tests whether candidates know the current legal position

concepts.name: Breach of Privilege: Definition, Categories, and Procedure
key_dimensions: Any act that obstructs a member in discharge of duties or obstructs the House in performing its functions constitutes breach
Categories: Direct breach (against a member) vs. Constructive breach (against the House as a body)
Procedure: Member raises matter → Speaker/Chairman decides if prima facie case exists → referred to Privileges Committee → Committee reports → House decides
UPSC trap: The Speaker/Chairman's decision to admit or reject a privilege motion is final and not subject to judicial review

concepts.name: Contempt of Parliament: Distinction from Breach of Privilege
key_dimensions: Contempt is broader than breach of privilege — any act that lowers the dignity or authority of the House even if no specific privilege is violated
Examples: Misrepresenting parliamentary proceedings, creating disturbance in galleries, publishing false reports of debates
Parliament is the sole judge of its contempt — no external authority can interfere
UPSC trap: Contempt of Parliament ≠ Contempt of Court — different bodies, different procedures, different punishments

concepts.name: Power to Punish for Breach: Imprisonment, Reprimand, and Expulsion
key_dimensions: Parliament can imprison, reprimand, admonish, or expel members — these are inherent powers, not derived from statute
Imprisonment by Parliament lasts only till the end of the session — House cannot imprison beyond its own session
Expulsion is the most severe punishment — but expelled member CAN contest elections (no constitutional bar)
UPSC trap: Courts cannot question the validity of expulsion (Tej Kiran Jain case) — judicial review is excluded for internal proceedings

concepts.name: Privileges of Strangers and Non-Members
key_dimensions: Privileges primarily belong to the House as a body, individual members, and certain officers — NOT to the general public
Strangers (visitors, journalists, lobbyists) can be excluded from proceedings at any time without giving reasons
Journalists reporting debates: Protected if reporting is fair and accurate, but House can prohibit publication
UPSC trap: A private individual who obstructs parliamentary business can also be punished for contempt even though they are not a member

concepts.name: Freedom from Arrest: Civil vs. Criminal Cases
key_dimensions: Members are free from arrest in CIVIL cases during session, 40 days before, and 40 days after — does NOT apply to criminal cases or preventive detention
Arrest in a civil case during this period is void — member must be released
No freedom from arrest in criminal cases — a member can be arrested and must notify the Speaker/Chairman
UPSC trap: The 40-day rule applies to civil suits ONLY — candidates frequently confuse this with criminal immunity

concepts.name: Right to Exclude Strangers and Conduct Secret Sittings
key_dimensions: Each House has the right to conduct its proceedings in secret — strangers (including press) can be asked to leave
Secret sitting procedure: Initiated by a minister or supported by at least 25 members (Lok Sabha Rules)
During secret sitting, no publication of proceedings is allowed — punishable as contempt
UPSC angle: This power is an inherent privilege, not derived from any specific article — tests knowledge of uncodified privileges

concepts.name: Privileges of Parliamentary Committees: Extent and Applicability
key_dimensions: Parliamentary committees enjoy the same privileges as the full House — proceedings before committees are protected
Evidence given before committees is privileged — witness cannot be sued for statements made
A member of the public giving false evidence before a parliamentary committee can be punished for contempt
UPSC trap: Privileges extend to proceedings of committees meeting OUTSIDE Parliament's premises if authorized by the House

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Parliamentary Privileges: Separation of Powers Tension
key_dimensions: Courts have traditionally held that they cannot question the internal proceedings of Parliament (Article 122/212)
However, courts CAN examine whether a privilege claimed actually exists — limited review is permissible
MSM Sharma vs. Krishna Sinha (1959): First major case — Supreme Court upheld Parliament's privilege over press publications
UPSC trap: Courts can check if the privilege is real, but cannot examine how the House exercised that privilege — a crucial distinction

concepts.name: Privileges vs. Fundamental Rights: The Conflict and Resolution
key_dimensions: Pre-Searchlight case position: Privileges were superior to Fundamental Rights
In Re: Under Article 143 (Special Reference): Supreme Court held privileges are part of constitutional framework and must be harmonized with Fundamental Rights
Article 105 is itself in the Constitution — so it operates as an exception to Part III rights in the parliamentary context
UPSC high-yield: Article 19(1)(a) (free speech) vs. Article 105(2) (parliamentary privilege over publication) — courts apply harmonious construction

concepts.name: Codification of Parliamentary Privileges: The Unresolved Constitutional Mandate
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment (1978) amended Article 105(3) to require Parliament to define its privileges by law — but Parliament has NOT done so in 45+ years
Result: Pre-Amendment position (House of Commons privileges as of 1950) continues to apply as a constitutional fiction
Arguments for codification: Legal certainty, prevent arbitrary use; Arguments against: Flexibility, cannot anticipate all situations
UPSC trap: Many candidates think privileges ARE codified — the fact that they are NOT is a frequently tested point

concepts.name: Privileges Related to Publication of Parliamentary Proceedings
key_dimensions: Parliamentary Papers Act (UK equivalent) — in India, the Houses have passed resolutions protecting publication of authorized reports
Unauthorized publication of secret session proceedings is contempt of Parliament
Authorized publication is absolutely privileged — no defamation suit can lie against the publisher
UPSC trap: A newspaper reporting parliamentary debates accurately is protected; selectively quoting to misrepresent is contempt

concepts.name: Speaker/Chairman's Role in Privilege Matters: Powers and Finality
key_dimensions: Speaker admits or rejects a privilege motion — this decision is quasi-judicial but final for the House's purposes
Speaker can also refer the matter directly to the Privileges Committee without a vote of the House
Speaker's decision on privilege is not subject to judicial review under Article 122
UPSC angle: Speaker's role creates accountability deficit — debates around need for an independent Privileges Committee

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law and Parliamentary Privilege: Intersection
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule (Anti-defection) gives the Speaker power to disqualify members — this is separate from privilege proceedings
A member's vote against party whip CANNOT be treated as breach of privilege by the party — Tenth Schedule governs, not privilege
Kihoto Hollohan case: Speaker's decisions under Tenth Schedule ARE subject to judicial review (unlike privilege decisions)
UPSC trap: Anti-defection decisions vs. privilege decisions have OPPOSITE positions on judicial review — a classic UPSC trap

concepts.name: Parliamentary Privilege and Lokpal/Anti-Corruption Investigations
key_dimensions: Post-Sita Soren (2024): Bribery of MPs now clearly outside the protection of privilege
Constitutional tension: Can CBI/ED investigate an MP's conduct related to parliamentary duties?
The act of accepting bribe is outside Parliament; the act of voting is inside — courts now distinguish clearly
UPSC relevance: Tests understanding of the boundary between parliamentary immunity and criminal accountability in contemporary context

concepts.name: Privileges of State Legislatures vs. Parliament: Similarities and Distinctions
key_dimensions: Article 194 mirrors Article 105 for state legislatures — same structure, same privileges
State legislatures have NOT codified privileges either — same default position applies
Key difference: State legislatures cannot claim privileges beyond what Parliament itself enjoys
UPSC trap: A state legislature claiming a privilege not available to Parliament = unconstitutional — tests comparative understanding

concepts.name: Privilege Motion Procedure: Admissibility Conditions and Parliamentary Practice
key_dimensions: Conditions for admissibility: Must relate to a member in their capacity as a member, must be raised at the earliest opportunity, must not be a matter already before a court
Speaker can reject a motion if it appears to be a political tactic rather than a genuine privilege concern
Recent trend: Privilege motions increasingly used as political tools — Committee rarely concludes proceedings
UPSC angle: The distinction between a 'calling attention motion' and a 'privilege motion' — both relate to accountability but differ in procedure and consequence
